name: Generation Effect
description: Information is usually remembered better when people generate it themselves than when they only read or receive it passively. Producing the answer, label, or completion tends to create a stronger memory trace than merely seeing it.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to onboarding, education, setup flows, note-taking, forms, and practice tasks. Products that make users actively produce, categorize, or retrieve something can often create better retention than passive walkthroughs alone.
prevalence_note: Common in learning science, edtech, and training design, but still secondary in general product-design canon compared with broader recognition/recall or cognitive-load heuristics.

findings.description: A large meta-analysis (126 articles, 310 experiments, 1,653 effect-size estimates) confirmed the generation effect is real for both item memory and context memory, and found that generation constraint (how constrained participants are in producing their response) significantly moderates the effect's magnitude -- a real, actionable design factor. The meta-analysis also evaluated 7 competing theoretical accounts of the mechanism, supporting some but not others, providing much stronger theoretical grounding than any single study could.
findings.source_title: Theories of the generation effect and the impact of generation constraint: A meta-analytic review

findings.description: Across multiple experiments and memory tests, items participants generated themselves were remembered better than matched items they only read, demonstrating a robust generation effect at encoding.
findings.source_title: The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory
